title: The Sleepy Dragon

before.title: The Sleepy Dragon
before.text:
A dragon slept under the hill for one hundred years. Grass grew over his door, and birds built homes above his nose.

One spring day, a girl named June heard a great sneeze. Smoke came out of the hill. She moved the grass and found the dragon.

"Is it morning?" he asked.

"It is a hundred years later," June said.

The dragon came outside. He was too sleepy to fly, so June brought him warm milk. He drank it in one long breath. Then he opened his wings and carried her over the village. Everyone looked up, but only June knew why the dragon was late.

title: The Pocket Forest

before.title: The Pocket Forest
before.text:
Sam bought a green coat at an old shop. In one pocket, he found a tiny tree. It had six leaves and a bird no bigger than his thumb.

He gave the tree one drop of water. At once, the pocket became deep and cool. Sam put in his hand and felt soft ground. The little bird flew around his fingers.

Each day, Sam cared for the pocket forest. He never took a branch or flower. In summer, he opened the pocket near his window, and fresh air filled his hot room. In winter, the small trees stayed green.

title: Peter Pan's Invitation

before.title: Peter Pan's Invitation
before.text:
Wendy was getting ready for bed when Peter Pan came through the open window. He had lost his shadow, and it lay near the curtain.

Wendy helped him put it back. Peter thanked her and told her about Neverland, where kids could fly and pirates went by boat the sea.

"Come with me," he said. Wendy looked at her sleeping brothers. The trip sounded wonderful, but she did not want to leave them.

Peter smiled. "They can come too."

Soon the three kids stood by the window. They thought of happy things, rose into the air, and followed Peter across the night sky.

after.title: Peter Pan's Invitation
after.text:
Wendy was getting ready for bed when Peter Pan came through the window. He had lost his shadow. Wendy found it and sewed it back to his foot.

Peter told her about Neverland, where there were pirates and children who could fly. “Come with me,” he said. Wendy wanted her brothers, John and Michael, to come too.

Peter said they could all go. He blew fairy dust over the children and told them to think happy thoughts. Soon they rose into the air and followed him through the night.

reason: Correct “pirates went by boat the sea,” and include the fairy dust needed for Wendy and her brothers to fly in Barrie’s work. Keep the invitation and shadow episode.

title: The Prince and the Pauper Trade Places

before.title: The Prince and the Pauper Trade Places
before.text:
Tom lived in a poor part of London. Edward lived inside a palace. They looked so much alike that people could not tell them apart.

When they met, they tried on each other's clothes for fun. Then a guard saw Tom in fine clothes and thought he was the prince. Edward, dressed in rags, was pushed into the street.

Tom learned that palace life was not easy. Edward learned how hard life was for poor children. When they finally met again, each boy understood the other's world. Edward became a kinder king because he remembered what he had seen outside the palace.

after.title: The Prince and the Pauper Trade Places
after.text:

When they met, they tried on each other’s clothes. Edward went out to speak to a guard. The guard saw his poor clothes, thought he was Tom, and pushed him away from the palace. Tom was left inside in Edward’s fine clothes.

Each boy faced a life he did not know. Tom had to act like a prince. Edward saw how hard life could be for poor people. Later, they found a way to tell the truth about who they were.

title: Anne's First Friend

One afternoon, Diana came from that house. She had dark hair and a quiet smile. Anne talked quickly about books, trees, and all the names she had given to places nearby.

Diana did not laugh. She listened, then showed Anne a path beside the stream.

Before they went home, the girls promised to be friends. Anne had arrived on the island by mistake, but that evening she felt that she belonged there.

title: Pollyanna's Window

before.title: Pollyanna's Window
before.text:
Pollyanna moved into her aunt's large, dark house. Her bedroom was small and had no picture on the wall. Her aunt thought she would complain.

Instead, Pollyanna opened the window. From there she could see trees, rooftops, and a bright piece of sky.

"A picture could not change," she said, "but this view changes every hour."

The next morning, rain covered the window. Pollyanna watched drops run down the glass and found shapes in them. Her aunt did not understand the game, but she began to notice the view too. Soon the curtains stayed open each day.

after.title: Pollyanna's Window
after.text:
Pollyanna came to live with her aunt. Her aunt gave her a small room under the roof. It had bare walls and no picture. Pollyanna felt sad at first.

Then she went to the window. Outside, she could see trees and the land beyond them. “This is my picture,” she thought. She opened the window and felt the fresh air.

Pollyanna played a game of finding something to be glad about, even on a hard day. She still missed the things she had wanted for her room. But she was glad to have its view.

reason: Porter’s book has the bare attic room, Pollyanna’s joy in its window view, and the glad game. The supplied rain scene and aunt opening curtains are invented; stay with the attested scene.

title: Sea Otters at Play

before.title: Otters at Play
before.text:
Two young otters played beside a rocky shore. One chased the other through the water. Then both rolled onto their backs and held small stones on their stomachs.

The stones were tools. The otters used them to break open hard shells. After eating, they hid the stones in loose skin under their arms.

As the tide carried them away, the otters held paws. This kept them from moving apart while they rested. They looked playful, but each action also helped them live safely in the cold sea.

after.title: Sea Otters at Play
after.text:
Two young sea otters swam beside a rocky shore. One chased the other through the water. Then an otter floated on its back and held a shell against its chest.

Some sea otters use a stone to break a hard shell. They can keep food in loose skin under their front legs while they swim.

Later, the two otters rested near floating kelp. Their play and their search for food were different parts of a day at sea.

reason: Specify sea otters; stone tools and underarm pockets are documented. Remove the claim that hand-holding is the general safety mechanism and end with an observed rest among kelp. The piece remains a composite explanatory scene, without individual names.

title: Seeds on the Wind

before.title: Seeds on the Wind
before.text:
A dandelion grows a white, round head after its yellow flower is gone. Each soft part holds one seed.

When the wind blows, the seeds rise into the air. Their light tops work like small umbrellas. Some fall close to the old plant. Others travel across a road or over a wall.

Most seeds do not find a good place. A few land on warm earth with enough water and light. Those seeds open and send down roots. In this way, a plant that cannot walk can still send its kids far from home.

after.title: Seeds on the Wind
after.text:

When the wind blows, the seeds can rise into the air. Their light tops work like little umbrellas. Some fall close to the old plant. Others travel across a road or over a wall.

Many seeds never grow. A few may land where they have enough water and light. New plants can grow there. This is one way a plant spreads its seeds without moving itself.

title: The Patient Heron

before.title: The Patient Heron
before.text:
A heron stood still beside a river. Small fish moved near its long legs, but the bird waited.

Another bird flew down and caught a little fish at once. "You are too slow," it called.

The sun moved higher. At last, a large fish came into the quiet water. The waiting bird moved its head as fast as an arrow and caught it.

The first bird had taken many little fish. The patient one needed only a single large fish. Each had found a way to get its meal.

before.text:

They planted again, although the season was already late. The harvest was smaller than usual, but every family received rice. The flood had damaged separate fields. Recovery began when the village treated them as one shared problem.

title: The Island's Power Cable

before.title: The Island's Power Cable
before.text:
A small island made electricity with an old oil machine. Fuel arrived by ship, and storms sometimes stopped the ships for weeks.

The island and the town on the coast planned a cable under the sea. It cost a great deal, and some people feared it would harm fish. Workers chose a path away from the main fishing grounds.

When the cable opened, the island had steady power. It still kept the old machine for emergencies. The new link made life easier, but careful planning protected the work that families had always done.

after.title: The Island's Power Cable
after.text:
This island is made up. It gets electricity from an old machine that needs fuel brought by ship. Storms sometimes delay the ships.

The island and a coastal town plan a cable under the sea. Engineers study where it might go. Fishers explain which places they use most, and the team changes part of its plan.

After the cable is ready, the island can get power from the coast. It keeps the old machine for times when the cable cannot be used. People continue to watch how the new route affects fishing.

title: A Vote from Far Away

before.title: A Vote from Far Away
before.text:
Lina moved overseas but still wanted to vote in her home country's election. The nearest office was six hours away.

This year, she could send her vote by mail. She read the rules, filled in the paper, and placed it inside two envelopes. Then she took it to the post office early.

For several days, Lina checked the delivery number. At last, the letter reached the election office. Her one vote did not decide everything, but distance had not taken away her voice. She called her mother, and they watched the results together.

after.title: A Vote from Far Away
after.text:

Lina sends it early and checks the letter’s delivery number. It reaches the election office before the deadline. She knows it must still be checked with the other ballots.

On election night, Lina calls her mother. They watch the results together, even though they live far apart.

reason: Overseas voting rules vary by country, and delivery confirmation does not prove a ballot was accepted. Present Lina’s example as fictional and distinguish mailing from the count.

One boy brought a clock that had belonged to his grandfather. It only needed a new spring. When the clock began to tick, the boy held it close to his ear. The table had saved more than an old object. It had saved a sound he remembered.

title: Dinner Without a Recipe

before.title: Dinner Without a Recipe
before.text:
Kai planned to cook soup, but he had forgotten to buy carrots. In the kitchen he found an onion, half a pumpkin, two tomatoes, and some beans.

He cut them up and put them in a pot. The soup looked too thick, so he added water. It tasted flat, so he added salt and a little lemon.

His sister came home and asked for a bowl. "What kind is it?" she said.

Kai had no answer. The soup had no recipe and no name, but they both asked for more.

after.text:

He cut up the vegetables and put them in a pot with the beans. The soup looked too thick, so he added water. It tasted flat, so he added salt and a little lemon.

His sister came home and asked for a bowl. “What kind is it?” she said.

Kai had no answer. The soup had no recipe and no name, but they both asked for more.

title: Bread in a Medieval Town

before.title: Bread in a Medieval Town
before.text:
Long ago, a large bread oven cost too much for one family. People in a town shared one instead.

Each morning, families made bread at home. They put a small mark on each piece so they could know it later. A baker took all the bread to the town oven.

One hot fire cooked food for the whole street and used less wood than many small fires. In the evening, each family came for its bread.

The pieces belonged to many homes, but the warmth came from one shared fire.

One morning, each family makes its dough at home. They press a small mark on their loaves so they can tell them apart. A baker helps place the bread in the hot oven.

Later, people return for their loaves. Neighbors talk while they wait. The oven belongs to the town, and this is the day they bake together.

title: The Ink Maker's Work

before.title: The Ink Maker's Work
before.text:
Before factories made bottles of ink, an ink maker needed patience. He gathered small hard balls that grew on oak trees after insects touched them.

He broke the balls, soaked them in water, and mixed the dark liquid with iron salt and tree gum. At first, the writing looked pale. Then air made it darker.

Writers liked this ink because it stayed on paper for years. The ink maker did not write the laws, letters, or poems of his time. Still, his careful work helped all of those words remain.

after.title: The Ink Maker's Work
after.text:
People once made writing ink from small round growths on oak trees. Insects help make these growths, called oak galls.

An ink maker could soak broken galls in water. Then the maker mixed the liquid with an iron compound and a little tree gum. The ink often grew darker after it touched the air.

Writers used this kind of ink for letters and records. The materials in the ink helped their words remain on paper for a long time.

reason: This explains iron gall ink ingredients and darkening over time; it is general nonfiction, not a dated narrative. Correct content type and subtopic. Oak galls arise after insects lay eggs and “iron salt” is better described simply as iron compound for this level.

One winter night, the bell rope broke during a storm. A girl from the tower keeper's family went up the stairs with a hammer. She struck the bell until the last ship entered safely. Her hands hurt, but every light returned to the harbor.

The village changed the plan. Each home gave either one day of work or a small amount of money. People who were old or sick brought lunch for the workers. The well stayed clean because there was more than one way to help.
